text:
*★☆☆☆☆ Beware of scammer “guides” and overpriced crafts at Sigiriya*

We visited Sigiriya Fortress today and had an amazing experience with the rock itself — but be warned about what happens when you come down.

*1. Fake local guides/scammers:* As soon as we got to the rock, multiple “local guides” surrounded us. They act friendly but are aggressive scammers pushing overpriced souvenirs and fake stories. If you want a real guide, book only through the official ticket counter or your hotel. The guide assisted us even didn't know correct information about the rock!!!

*2. Overpriced art & crafts trap:* The same people sell “handmade” art and crafts right at the exit area, claiming “special price for tourists”. We bought a few items feeling pressured. Later we checked the *official art & craft shop at the Sigiriya Museum* and found the *exact same items for 3-4x lower prices*, with proper fixed prices and no haggling.

*Tips to avoid this:*
- *Say a firm “No, thank you”* and keep walking when approached at the bottom.
- *Do NOT buy crafts at the exit.* Wait and buy from the museum shop or shops in Dambulla/Habarana town where prices are fair and marked.
- *If you need a guide, hire only at the main entrance* with an official ID badge.

Sigiriya is world-class, but these scammers ruin the experience. Authorities should control this. Tourists — save your money and buy at the museum shop instead.

text:
Sigiriya Lion Rock is absolutely worth visiting, even though the entrance fee is quite expensive. It’s one of those places that truly lives up to the hype.
I highly recommend arriving before 9:00 AM. After that, the site gets very crowded with tourists, and both the walking paths and the climb become slow and congested. Going early makes the experience much more enjoyable, cooler, and more peaceful.

Be careful with food and drinks—there are quite a few cheeky monkeys around, and they will try to grab anything they can!

The climb itself is a bit challenging but manageable, and once you reach the top, the view is simply breathtaking. You get a stunning panoramic view of the surrounding jungle and landscapes, which makes all the effort completely worth it. The historical ruins at the summit are also fascinating historical.
Overall, a must-visit destination if you’re in Sri Lanka—just plan ahead and go early for the best experience.

text:
"Sigiriya is not just a destination; it is a breathtaking encounter with ancient Sri Lankan brilliance. Rising 200 meters from the central plains, this massive rock fortress was the royal capital of King Kashyapa in the 5th century. It is a masterpiece of urban planning, hydraulic engineering, and artistic expression that truly earns its title as the 'Eighth Wonder of the World.'
What to See and Experience
The Water Gardens: As you enter, you are greeted by symmetrically designed pleasure gardens and advanced hydraulic systems that still function today—a marvel of ancient engineering.
The Mirror Wall: Once polished so thoroughly that the King could see his reflection, it is now covered in 'Sigiri Graffiti,' poems written by ancient visitors from centuries ago.
The Frescoes: Halfway up the rock, you will find the world-famous frescoes of the 'Sigiri Ladies.' These vibrant paintings have survived for over 1,500 years and represent the peak of ancient Sri Lankan art.
The Lion’s Paw: The final ascent starts between two massive lion paws carved into the rock, which is all that remains of a colossal lion statue that once guarded the entrance.
The Summit: Reaching the top reveals the ruins of the royal palace and a 360-degree panoramic view of the lush jungles and mountains. The sunset from here is absolutely spiritual.
Essential Tips for Travelers
Timing is Key: Start your climb as early as possible (around 7:00 AM) or late in the afternoon (3:30 PM) to avoid the scorching heat and the heavy crowds.
Hydration: Carry plenty of water, but please ensure you use reusable bottles to minimize plastic waste.
Footwear: Wear sturdy, comfortable walking shoes. There are roughly 1,200 steps to the summit, and some sections can be steep and narrow.
The Wasp Warning: At the Lion’s Paw area, be mindful of signs regarding wasps. Avoid making loud noises or wearing strong perfumes, as these can disturb them.
Hire a Guide: To truly appreciate the history, consider hiring a licensed guide at the entrance. Their stories bring the ruins to life.
Respect and Sustainability
As travelers, we must be guardians of this heritage:
Strictly No Photography: Taking photos of the Frescoes is strictly prohibited to protect the ancient pigments from camera flashes. Please respect this rule.
Leave No Trace: Sigiriya is a sensitive ecological area. Do not litter, and do not feed the monkeys. Let’s keep this ancient wonder pristine for future generations.
Cultural Respect: Dress modestly and be mindful of the sacred nature of the historical sites.
Whether you are a history buff, a photography enthusiast, or an adventure seeker, Sigiriya offers an experience that is both physically challenging and intellectually rewarding. It is the crown jewel of Sri Lanka's Cultural Triangle and a journey you will never forget!"

There are 1,200 steps to climb, and if you start from the garden at the bottom, it seems to be well over 1,200. It takes about two hours. The steps are all different widths and small, making it quite challenging. People with a fear of heights should definitely not climb. It's extremely hot, so I recommend visiting early in the morning. Be sure to bring water. The lion's paws are visible around the middle. Tour groups are very crowded around lunchtime. The symmetrical gardens from the summit are breathtaking. If you catch a good tuk-tuk, you can even take a photo spot with a stunning view of Sigiriya without having to climb up to Pidurangala. You can see the celestial woman mural on the way down, but the cave is very small and photography is prohibited, which is a shame. Still, I'm so glad I reached the summit of Sigiriya!!!

Very touristy and crowded.
Except at opening time, 5 a.m., when you can enjoy it more, but the start of the walk is in the dark...
The climb, especially towards the end, can be quite impressive (beware of vertigo). If the weather is clear, it must be exceptional; in the mist, the surrounding view is limited!

text:
Unfortunately, I can't give more than two stars.

Safety is never truly guaranteed. The same narrow staircases are used for both ascent and descent, which is problematic given the number of visitors. Furthermore, some of the stairs and railings are visibly rusted through, which doesn't inspire confidence.

In my opinion, the price-performance ratio is completely unacceptable. I paid 11,800 Sri Lankan rupees, while locals only pay 120 rupees. This enormous price difference is incomprehensible to me.

I have no idea what the money is used for, as there is a lack of information about the historical structures. There are hardly any signs explaining what was there previously or what the sites originally looked like, and as already mentioned, safety is extremely inadequate.

The view was nice, but I actually preferred the view from Pidurangala Rock, as it offers an impressive view of Sigiriya Lion Rock.

Overall, I had much higher expectations.

text:
Sigiriya, a green plateau with forests, crops, and lakes, is located in north-central Sri Lanka, 180 km from Colombo.
Around the 5th century AD, King Kashyapa built a fortified palace on a huge 180-meter-high monolith of hardened magma, which, like others, stands out above a plain rich in plants and lakes about 200 meters above sea level.
At the summit, a sumptuous palace, hanging gardens, and water cisterns supplied by an ingenious hydraulic system that still functions when it rains.
The walls were frescoed with the famous "Maidens of Sigiriya," all with large dolls, perhaps concubines. Around the base of the rock were two canals filled with water, which served as reservoirs and as defense, given the resident crocodiles.
In short, an incredible place to inspire the imagination.
The entrance was carved in the shape of a seated lion, of which only the paws now remain, and from there one climbed 1,200 steps to the summit.
The old area facing the rock has been equipped to accommodate the many guests and offers two options: climbing the rock for $35, or just visiting the museum for $6.
Had I still been vigorous, I would have climbed the 1,200 steps without a problem.
Sigiriya, considered the eighth wonder of the world, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1982 for its combination of urban planning, architecture, hydraulic technology, and art.
So I toured the rock by tuktuk for 6,000 lkr, seeing it from all sides, along with another nearby rock, surrounded by greenery and plenty of water.
Then I toured the museum, with lots of photos from early 19th-century archaeologists, various tomb finds and things from a later Buddhist monastery, all stuff you find everywhere in Italy, and a wall repainted with images of the 'Sigiriya maidens'.

text:
Beautiful place with great scenic and as well as archeological / historical value. (And also a UNESCO listed site).
Commonly known as "Sigiriya" or the "Lion's rock".
Built by King Kashyapa, who is the son of King Datusena of Anuradhapura kingdom of Sri Lanka.
When king Kashyapa choose sigiriya as his fortress, there was a buddhist monastery at the Sigiriya. Then the Kashyapa had to replace the monks to the near monastic site of "Pidurangala". Then king Kashyapa built his mind blowing castle on top of the lion's rock. Today you can see the ruins of that old buildings on the top and few ponds as well.

At the bottom, the water gardens and the boulder gardens were architect with great precision and accuracy. The water fountains at the water garden are still working even today which are thousands of years old. It's amazing to visit those buildings and monuments which built with great technology and architecture.
And the other most famous thing of the Sigiriya is " The Frescose ". Those are very beautiful and colorful paintings. Must see stuff. Apart from those conserved frescose, there are many other fragmented ones can be seen on the cave tops at the bottom site.

Many people are climbing up early in the morning to see the sunrises from the top and same as for the evenings. Bit crowded around that particular time periods. But other times, not too many crowd. During those time you can visit the site peacefully.

And specially, there are many different specieses of birds and wildlife can be spotted. (The macaques - little brown coloured monkeys are everywhere at the site same as many other touris attractions. So please be careful). It's great that the Central Cultural Fund (CCF) of Sri Lanka is taking good care of the site.
Must visit place in Sri Lanka that exhibit the great architectural and artistic wonders of ancient Sri Lanka.
